subject: European History
title: 8. First World War, Peace Settlement and League of Nations

segments.text: The war became a prolonged industrial struggle because modern firepower favoured defence and no early offensive produced decisive victory; the peace settlement then tried to solve security, borders and reparations simultaneously but created new tensions, and the League of Nations lacked the power and universal participation needed to guarantee collective security.

Germany’s initial strategy failed to produce quick victory, leading to entrenched trench warfare from the North Sea to Switzerland, where machine guns, artillery and barbed wire made offensive warfare extraordinarily costly; fighting also occurred across Eastern Europe, the Balkans, the Ottoman Empire, Africa and the Middle East, making this a genuinely global conflict involving colonial troops and resources. Governments controlled industry, labour, food and finance on an unprecedented scale — total war drew civilian populations deeply into rationing, propaganda, labour and mass casualty. The

The League provided forums for diplomacy, administered mandates, and pursued collective security, but lacked its own military power and suffered from the United States’ absence and great-power reluctance to enforce sanctions — weaknesses that became especially visible in the 1930s (Topic 9). It should not, however, be dismissed as entirely useless; it achieved real successes in smaller disputes and humanitarian work even while failing against major-power aggression.

items.text: The 1919 settlement imposing territorial loss, military restriction, reparations and the war-guilt clause on Germany.
The interwar collective-security organisation lacking its own military force and full great-power participation.

Make one “war turning points” page and one “peace settlement” page; for Versailles, separate territorial, military, economic and political provisions before evaluating criticism against the real security problems peacemakers faced.

Practise one analytical outline answering: “Judge the Treaty of Versailles against the problems it tried to solve — security, borders, reparations, self-determination — rather than a simple success/failure verdict.”
Do not limit WWI to trench warfare in France; other fronts and global dimensions mattered.
Do not say Versailles alone “caused Hitler”; economic crisis, political instability and Nazi agency also mattered (Topic 9).
Do not describe the League as completely useless; distinguish its real smaller achievements from its failure against major aggression.
The First World War began in 1914 and ended with the armistice of 11 November 1918.
The United States entered the war in 1917; Russia left after the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in 1918.
The Paris Peace Conference opened in 1919 and produced the Treaty of Versailles among others.
The League of Nations was created for collective security, but the United States never joined.
Judge the peace settlement by the problems it tried to solve and the contradictions it could not resolve, not by a simple success/failure label.
The League’s real but limited achievements should be weighed against its well-documented failure against major-power aggression — both facts belong in a balanced answer.
